publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Microwave Filters and Antennas for Personal Communication Systems
abstract: Describes tunable ring resonator filter elements, with potential applications in personal communications systems. The simple microstrip ring resonator consists of a closed loop of microstrip. Such resonators have lower Q factors than dielectric puck or YIG resonators but they are adequate for many filter applications, and have a particular advantage in the context of personal communications in that they are compatible with surface mount technology. In the typical case when the line width is small compared to the radius, the resonant modes can be determined by simple transmission line theory. Ring resonators can be made tunable by mounting variable capacitance diodes across gaps in the ring, or to ground from suitable points on the ring. Tuning curves for several configurations are discussed. Theoretical and practical results are given for a 1.8 GHz element. Low-cost MMIC amplifiers are incorporated to compensate for resonator losses, and novel features are included to reduce higher frequency resonances. The active devices are mounted inside the ring to minimize the size.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Microwave Filters and Antennas for Personal Communication Systems
abstract: The inverted-F antenna, for personal communication networks (PCN), was characterised by looking into their matching techniques and by measuring their overall radiation patterns at 1.8 GHz. Besides the readiness of matching this type of antenna it was shown that its radiation pattern is rather directional. This interesting feature, should it be exploited properly, could provide a better signal reception as well as better protection to the user body. It is felt that this is achievable by controlling, to a certain limit, the structure dimensions and/or the shape of the handset ground plane.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Band switched patch radiators for telephone handsets
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Microwave Filters and Antennas for Personal Communication Systems
abstract: The performance of several antenna types for use with telephone handsets is examined. Radiation patterns are presented for telephones when handheld and when in free space and the quarter wavelength patch antenna is found particularly attractive. Unfortunately the bandwidth is insufficient for some applications so electrical tuning is considered in those cases. The design of a band switched patch radiator to separate the transmit and receive functions for personal communication networks (PCN) is presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Supergain array containing only one fed element at 1.8 GHz
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Microwave Filters and Antennas for Personal Communication Systems
abstract: The authors report the development of a supergrain array of four dipoles containing only one-fed element operating at 1.8 GHz. The array has a length of 0.6 lambda and occupies an area of 8.4*10 cm/sup 2/ at 1.8 GHz. The array, designed using maximum gain theorem, produces a gain of 7.8 dBd with a 0.5 dB bandwidth of 2.5%. Such array may find applications in narrow band personal communication systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: GaAs MMIC active filters for L-band mobile systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Microwave Filters and Antennas for Personal Communication Systems
abstract: MMIC technology is the key to making microwave and millimetre-wave transceivers affordable for widespread use in applications such as wireless data communications, and micro/pico-cellular mobile communications. Active filters could have an important part to play in the miniaturisation of handheld terminals and advanced satellite payloads for mobile systems. This paper describes and compares three techniques which have been used for the realisation of MMIC active filters operating in the 1-2 GHz region. The advantages and disadvantages of these active filters are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Switched dual mode patch antennas for mobile systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Microwave Filters and Antennas for Personal Communication Systems
abstract: Many new satellite based services are planned for road vehicles including telephone and data communications, vehicle positioning systems and traffic information. Compact antennas are required to receive all these services. These must be cheap to manufacture, as conformal as possible with the vehicle, offer multiple frequency band operation and a variety of radiation patterns to operate with both geostationary and continuously orbiting satellites. Here the properties of annular ring microstrip patch antennas operating at higher order modes are assessed for use on vehicles in mobile communication systems. The antennas have been studied both theoretically and experimentally to examine the radiated beam shape, gain and the bandwidth for several methods of feeding. The performance of rings printed on different substrates and a glass superstrate are examined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Mobile antenna systems-highlights of recent developments in personal communication equipment
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Microwave Filters and Antennas for Personal Communication Systems
abstract: The important role of antennas in mobile communication systems is emphasised and in particular the difficulties encountered when the equipment is mounted near or on the human body. Antenna system design problems are identified and a selection highlighted by examples of recent equipment. The present situation is summarised and likely future trends considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
